Bookshelf

Suggested reading in philosophy and business.

I haven’t necessarily read these, and the tiers aren’t my ratings. Open a book to see a note on it and its suggested tier.

S

GGood Strategy/Bad StrategyRichard Rumelt

Rumelt argues that a good strategy names the real problem, picks an approach to it, and lines up actions behind that approach.

Start here for consulting and product work, especially when a plan is full of vague business language.

About the book
TThe Sciences of the ArtificialHerbert A. Simon

Simon writes about designed systems and how they fit their environment, and about deciding with limited information.

Economics and AI both come up, through the question of how to design things.

About the book
TThinking in SystemsDonella H. Meadows

A short introduction to stocks, flows, feedback loops and delays, and what happens when you change a system.

A data pipeline changes how people work and what they get rewarded for, and this book helps you think that through.

About the book
TThe Beginning of InfinityDavid Deutsch

Deutsch argues that knowledge grows through explanation and criticism, and that progress could keep going.

The account of how knowledge improves fits practical work as well as philosophy.

About the book
77 PowersHamilton Helmer

Helmer describes seven conditions that let a business keep an advantage that competitors can’t copy.

Use it to ask what would stop competitors from copying an AI product or services business.

About the book

A

HHigh Output ManagementAndrew S. Grove

Grove explains how a manager measures output, sets up processes, runs meetings and develops people.

A founder taking on more projects and more people will get the most from it.

About the book
TThe Mom TestRob Fitzpatrick

A short guide to asking customers about their past behavior, since people tend to be polite about your idea.

Read it before any customer interview, for product or consulting work.

About the book
TThe Effective ExecutivePeter F. Drucker

Drucker covers how executives spend their time, set priorities, use their strengths and make decisions.

The advice on getting useful work done fits most business and product jobs.

About the book
SSeeing Like a StateJames C. Scott

Scott looks at large planning schemes that forced simple administrative models onto complicated local life.

Keep it in mind on any automation project that might ignore how people on the ground do the work.

About the book
FFinite and Infinite GamesJames P. Carse

Carse separates games played to win from games played to keep the game going.

It raises the question of which business goals are worth chasing. It’s written in short aphorisms.

About the book
AAntifragileNassim Nicholas Taleb

Taleb writes about systems that get stronger from shocks, and argues for keeping options open and limiting the downside.

Its ideas fit running experiments well. The big claims deserve some skepticism.

About the book
TThe Nicomachean EthicsAristotle

Aristotle on living well, virtue, friendship and practical judgment.

Aristotle treats character as something you build by practicing, which fits a discipline like karate.

About the book

B

ZZero to OnePeter Thiel with Blake Masters

Thiel argues that startups should build something new.

Check its strongest claims against real customers and market data before acting on them.

About the book
TThe Innovator’s DilemmaClayton M. Christensen

Christensen explains why well-run incumbents can lose ground when disruptive technologies arrive.

It helps explain how incumbents adopt AI. The strategy books in higher tiers are more practical.

About the book
TThe Structure of Scientific RevolutionsThomas S. Kuhn

Kuhn describes normal science, the anomalies it can’t explain, and how scientific paradigms change.

Some of it carries over to how technology changes, though science and startups only compare so far.

About the book
MMeditationsMarcus Aurelius

Marcus Aurelius’s private Stoic notes on judgment, duty, how nothing lasts, and how to act.

Read it for discipline and staying calm. The short entries are easy to reread.

About the book
OOn LibertyJohn Stuart Mill

Mill argues for individual freedom and open debate, and for limits on how far society can interfere with a person.

It’s about thinking and writing for yourself, and it leaves room to question how the principles work inside institutions and online.

About the book

C

RReasons and PersonsDerek Parfit

Long, detailed arguments about rationality, personal identity, morality and what we owe people over time.

It’s dense and slow to get through alongside other projects. That time is why it sits in C tier.

About the book
TThe Sovereignty of GoodIris Murdoch

Three essays on goodness, on how we see other people, and on the limits of ethics built around the will.

There’s little direct business advice in it.

About the book
TThe GoalEliyahu M. Goldratt with Jeff Cox

A business novel about a manufacturing plant’s problems that explains the theory of constraints.

The bottleneck ideas apply directly to operations. The story takes longer to read than a short summary of the theory would.

About the book
